structure.rationale: The order follows how a fork-based risk engine is built and used: first the market objects it prices off (curves and conventions), then what it measures on them (risk measures), the instruments it holds (Treasuries, futures, SOFR swaps), and the time/funding effects that move value without a market move (carry, roll, funding). Liquidity and scenarios then say what trading costs and which futures to test; hedging and optimization turn those into trades; data operations and governance cover feeding the engine and trusting its output. Chapters are the requester's nine, kept in their order; each is told as one scene in plain words per the Thing Explainer voice, with the real term quoted once.
structure.audience: A team building a fixed-income fork-based risk engine, assumed to know bonds and swaps at a working level but needing the trading-desk and bank-governance context around them.
structure.status: skeleton: sources are structure anchors named in book.json notes plus primary-data/docs pointers; URLs and claims are to be verified by each concept step before use

claims.text: US Treasury notes and bonds use Actual/Actual (ICMA): accrued fraction = actual days since last coupon / (days in coupon period x coupons per year); a 182-day half-year gives a 364 denominator.

SOFR fixed-vs-floating swaps trade with annual payments on both legs, both ACT/360 (fixed leg too). The 30/360 semi-annual fixed leg is the legacy LIBOR-era convention; cleared venues permit other fixed day counts, so confirm per trade.
Brief lists 30/360 for fixed swap legs; for SOFR swaps the market convention is ACT/360 annual, so the page teaches 30/360 as the older/other-currency convention and flags the difference.
Log-linear interpolation of discount factors is the same as piecewise-constant forward rates between nodes (forwards jump at nodes).

Monotone convex (Hagan & West) keeps continuous forwards positive when input discrete forwards are positive and preserves monotonicity regions; it reproduces each period's discrete forward by integration.
Dirty price = clean price + accrued interest; Treasuries trade on clean price and regular-way settle next business day (T+1) — common market practice, not confirmed from a fetched primary source.
Treasury publishes a daily par yield curve (CMT) at fixed tenors from on-the-run securities; fitted-spline approaches use all bonds.
SOFR is a published overnight rate; SOFR OIS compounds it daily and is the standard USD discounting curve for cleared swaps.
QuantLib objects: YieldTermStructure (curve base), RelinkableYieldTermStructureHandle, SimpleQuote, Observer/Observable; curves are LazyObject and recompute when a quote changes.

snippets.code:
q = ql.SimpleQuote(0.0425)
h = ql.QuoteHandle(q)
helper = ql.OISRateHelper(2, ql.Period('5Y'), h, sofr_index)
curve = ql.PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount(today, [helper], ql.Actual365Fixed())
handle = ql.RelinkableYieldTermStructureHandle(curve)
q.setValue(0.0430)  # curve notices, rebuilds on next query
snippets.note: Pattern from QuantLib docs/cookbook; not executed here — check class names against installed QuantLib version.

pitfalls: Using ACT/360 vs ACT/ACT for a quote moves rates by roughly 1.4% of the rate — silently wrong carry.
Accrued interest uses coupon-period length, so it differs between semiannual periods of 181-184 days.
Log-linear discount interpolation gives sawtooth forwards; bumping one node shifts forwards unevenly.
Forgetting that a 'next business day' settlement date changes accrued interest on Fridays/holidays.
Relinking a handle changes every dependent instrument — intended for forks, but easy to share by accident.

claims.text: DV01 = modified duration x price x 0.0001: the dollar value change for a one basis point move. Sign convention varies; state it (here: DV01 is the loss for +1bp, positive for a long bond).
Portfolio DV01 is the sum of position DV01s when all use the same parallel shift of the same curve; it hides offsetting exposures at different tenors.
Key-rate DV01 uses a triangular bump peaking at a key tenor and tapering linearly to neighbours, estimated by central difference (P- minus P+) / 2; partial durations sum to the parallel duration.
Bumping par (market quote) rates and re-bootstrapping gives risk per instrument a trader can hedge; bumping zero rates gives risk per curve node. Choice is a convention that must be stated.

Duration and convexity are the first two Taylor terms; accuracy falls as shock size grows; sources suggest adding convexity beyond ~25-50bp, and full revaluation for large shocks, curve-shaped scenarios and optionality.
Bump size must be small enough to be local but large enough to avoid numerical noise; 1bp central difference is a common convention, not a rule.
Hedging with DV01 alone removes first-order parallel risk only; convexity and curve-shape risk remain.
Curve-shape shocks: bull/bear = yields down/up; steepener/flattener = long-minus-short spread widens/narrows; butterfly = belly moves vs wings. Level, slope, curvature are the usual PCA factors.
P&L attribution splits change in value into carry, roll-down, curve move, spread change and an unexplained residual.

snippets.code: 10y, 4% semiannual coupon bond at 4% yield, price 100: DV01 = 0.0818 per 100 face; convexity ~ 78.9 (in yield-squared units, per 100 price: 7889.8/100); +25bp: full -2.0195, DV01-only -2.0439, DV01+convexity -2.0193; +100bp: full -7.7946, DV01-only -8.1757, with convexity -7.7812; +200bp: full -14.877, DV01-only -16.351, with convexity -14.773.
snippets.note: Computed by the author in Python from the bond price formula on 2026-10-08.

pitfalls: Mixing sign conventions between systems flips hedges.
Summing DV01 across currencies/curves without a common curve.
Bumping zero rates when the desk hedges with par instruments.
Too-small bumps give noise; one-sided bumps bias with convexity.
Taylor on instruments with optionality or large curve-shape shocks.
Residual in attribution is a signal of a bug, not noise to hide.
